analogy.p: Imagine a factory with solar panels on its roof (chlorophyll in chloroplasts). Raw materials arrive by two routes: a delivery road for water (the xylem) and an air vent for carbon dioxide (the stomata). Using the solar energy, the factory assembles sugar and releases oxygen as a by-product, then stores spare sugar in a warehouse as starch. The analogy works because it shows energy in, raw materials in, product and waste out. It breaks down because a real factory is built by people and needs workers, whereas the leaf's 'machinery' is organelles and enzymes working without being directed.

bullets: Photosynthesis happens in **green plants and algae** (and some bacteria such as cyanobacteria).
It is **endothermic**: energy is **taken in** from the environment (light), and stored as chemical energy in glucose.
The reactants are **carbon dioxide and water**; the products are **glucose and oxygen**.
**Producers** make the biomass that all other organisms in food chains depend on, so photosynthesis is the basis of nearly all life on Earth.
The oxygen released supports **aerobic respiration** in plants, animals and many microorganisms.
Link: it is the opposite of **aerobic respiration**, which releases energy from glucose using oxygen.
core.p: **Photosynthesis** is the process by which green plants and algae make their own food. It is an **endothermic reaction**, which means it takes in energy from the surroundings: here the energy is **light energy**, transferred from the environment to the **chloroplasts**. This light energy is used to join carbon dioxide and water into **glucose**, with **oxygen** produced as a by-product. Because plants and algae make their own food from simple inorganic substances they are called **producers**.

bullets: **Word equation:** carbon dioxide + water → (light) glucose + oxygen.
**Symbol equation:** 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
**Check the balance:** carbon 6 = 6; hydrogen 12 = 12; oxygen 12 + 6 = 18 on the left and 6 + 12 = 18 on the right.
Light energy and **chlorophyll** are needed but are **not reactants**, so they are written on the arrow, not in the equation.
Common exam trap: do not write the arrow as a reversible reaction; photosynthesis is a one-way reaction (respiration is its reverse in terms of reactants/products).
The ratio is **6 : 6 : 1 : 6**, so one molecule of glucose is made from six molecules of carbon dioxide.
core.p: You must be able to write both equations from memory. The word equation is carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with 'light' written above the arrow. The balanced symbol equation is **6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂**. The number six in front of the molecules is needed to balance the atoms on each side. Always write 'light' and 'chlorophyll' on or under the arrow when asked for the full conditions.

bullets: **Chloroplasts** contain **chlorophyll**, which absorbs light (mainly red and blue, reflecting green).
Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts and sit **near the top of the leaf** where they absorb the most light.
**Root cells and most cells in non-green parts have no chloroplasts**.
Algae (including seaweed and phytoplankton) also have chloroplasts and photosynthesise; they are the main producers in aquatic habitats.
Link: this is why **variegated leaves** (green and white) only make starch in the green parts.
Chloroplasts are a **sub-cellular structure** you met in cell biology: plant cells have them, animal cells do not.
core.h: Where photosynthesis happens: chloroplasts and chlorophyll
core.p: Photosynthesis takes place inside **chloroplasts**, the green organelles found in the cells of leaves and some stems. Chloroplasts contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which **absorbs light energy** and transfers it to the reaction. Not all plant cells have chloroplasts: root cells are underground, away from light, so they contain none. Cells in the leaf, especially the **palisade mesophyll**, contain the most chloroplasts.

bullets: **Broad, flat shape**: a large surface area to absorb more light.
**Thin leaf**: a short diffusion distance for CO₂ to reach the cells.
**Palisade mesophyll**: tightly packed, many chloroplasts, near the top surface, so most light is absorbed here.
**Spongy mesophyll**: has **air spaces** so CO₂ can diffuse easily to the cells and oxygen can leave.
**Stomata** (pores, mostly on the lower surface) let CO₂ in and oxygen out; **guard cells** open and close them, controlling water loss.
**Xylem** brings water from the roots; **phloem** carries away the sugars (translocation).
**Transparent upper epidermis** and a waxy **cuticle** let light through and reduce water loss.
core.h: How the leaf is adapted for photosynthesis
core.p: A leaf is an **organ** designed for photosynthesis. It is flat and thin, giving a large surface area for absorbing light and a short distance for gases to diffuse. Different tissues work together: epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem, phloem and guard cells. Learning how each layer helps is a common exam question.

bullets: **CO₂** diffuses in through open stomata, down its concentration gradient, as it is used up inside the leaf.
**Water** is taken up by root hair cells by **osmosis**, then moves up the **xylem** vessels to the leaf.
**Light** comes from the Sun (or lamps in experiments); the amount is measured as **light intensity**.
**Minerals** (nitrates, magnesium) are not used to make glucose itself but are needed for making proteins and chlorophyll.
A plant that cannot get one input cannot photosynthesise at full rate; whichever is scarcest becomes the **limiting factor**.
Only a small fraction of the light energy reaching a leaf is stored; the rest is reflected, transmitted or lost as heat.
core.h: Raw materials: how the plant obtains them
core.p: A plant must get carbon dioxide, water and light. **Carbon dioxide** enters through the stomata by diffusion from the air. **Water** is absorbed from the soil by osmosis through root hair cells and carried up the xylem to the leaves. **Light** is absorbed by chlorophyll. Understanding these inputs helps you explain limiting factors in the next spec point.

bullets: **Respiration**: glucose is used in aerobic respiration to release energy for the plant's life processes.
**Starch**: glucose is converted to insoluble starch for storage (in leaves, roots, stems), because starch does not affect osmosis and is compact.
**Cellulose**: used to make strong **cell walls** for new cells (growth).
**Fats or oils**: stored in seeds as an energy store (for example sunflower, rapeseed).
**Amino acids**: glucose combined with **nitrate ions** absorbed from the soil forms amino acids, which are built into **proteins**.
Storing as **insoluble starch** prevents glucose dissolving and drawing water into cells by osmosis.
Link: energy stored in starch is later released by respiration, for example at night or when seeds germinate.
core.h: What happens to the glucose: uses of glucose
core.p: The glucose produced is a **soluble sugar** that can be used or converted to other substances. Some is used immediately in **respiration** to release energy. The rest is converted to substances used for growth or stored for later. You need to know the main uses of glucose in plants and why each is needed.

bullets: **Step 1:** dip the leaf in **boiling water** for about 10 seconds to **kill the cell** and stop chemical reactions, and soften the leaf.
**Step 2:** place the leaf in a boiling tube of **ethanol** in a **hot water bath** (Bunsen burner off) to **remove the chlorophyll**.
**Step 3:** rinse the leaf in **cold water** to soften it again.
**Step 4:** spread the leaf on a white tile and add a few drops of **iodine solution**.
**Result:** blue-black = starch present; orange-brown = no starch.
**Variegated leaf**: green areas turn blue-black, white areas stay orange-brown, showing chlorophyll is needed.
**Safety:** ethanol is highly flammable (no naked flames); wear eye protection; iodine stains; boiling water is a scald hazard.
**Destarching:** the plant is first left in the dark for 24 to 48 hours to use up existing starch, so any starch found was made during the experiment.
core.h: Testing a leaf for starch (practical skills)
core.p: Because glucose made in photosynthesis is converted to starch, finding starch in a leaf shows that photosynthesis has occurred. **Iodine solution** is orange-brown and turns **blue-black** when starch is present. To see the colour change the green chlorophyll must be removed first. This method is a common practical-skills question and the safety steps are marked.

bullets: **Light:** foil covers part of the leaf; only the uncovered area turns blue-black.
**Carbon dioxide:** one plant in a sealed bag with soda lime or sodium hydroxide solution (absorbs CO₂); a control plant without it. The CO₂-free leaf has no starch.
**Chlorophyll:** variegated leaf; only green parts contain starch.
Oxygen release can be shown with **pondweed**: bubbles of gas collected are oxygen (tested with a glowing splint relighting).
Use a **control** each time so you can compare, and keep other variables constant.
Remember to **destarch** the plant first or the results are not valid.
core.p: Simple experiments show that light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll are needed. To show that light is needed, cover part of a destarched leaf with foil. To show that carbon dioxide is needed, enclose a plant with soda lime (absorbs CO₂). To show chlorophyll is needed, use a variegated leaf. In each case the starch test is the final indicator.

bullets: **Photosynthesis:** takes in CO₂ and water, releases O₂, **endothermic**, only in cells with chloroplasts, only in light.
**Respiration:** takes in O₂ and glucose, releases CO₂ and water, **exothermic**, in all living cells, all the time.
In **bright light**: net uptake of CO₂ and net release of O₂.
In **darkness**: net uptake of O₂ and release of CO₂.
When the two rates are equal there is **no net gas exchange**.
This is why a pondweed experiment gives fewer bubbles in dim light.
core.p: Plants photosynthesise only in light, but they respire all the time (day and night) because their cells always need energy. In bright light, photosynthesis happens faster than respiration, so the plant takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen overall. In dim light the two balance, and in darkness only respiration occurs, so the plant takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide like an animal.

bullets: **Food:** plants and algae are the producers at the start of food chains; the energy comes from the Sun.
**Oxygen:** photosynthesis maintains oxygen in the atmosphere needed for aerobic respiration.
**Carbon dioxide:** it removes CO₂ (a greenhouse gas), so deforestation reduces this uptake.
**Carbon cycle:** photosynthesis moves carbon from the air into plant biomass.
**Fossil fuels** store energy that originally came from sunlight via photosynthesis.
Farmers/growers increase yield by controlling limiting factors (for example light, CO₂ and temperature in greenhouses), linked to the next spec point.
core.h: Importance of photosynthesis: food, oxygen and carbon dioxide
core.p: Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and releases oxygen. The glucose made becomes **biomass** that feeds every consumer in a food chain. Fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas were formed from the remains of organisms that photosynthesised millions of years ago. Understanding this connects photosynthesis to ecology, the carbon cycle and climate change.

bullets: **Endothermic** = energy is transferred **from the environment** to the reacting system.
In photosynthesis the energy source is **light**, absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts.
The energy is stored in the **chemical bonds of glucose**, ready to be released later in respiration.
Bond breaking in the reactants takes more energy than is released forming the products.
Exam wording: 'energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light'.
Link: **respiration** is exothermic and releases the stored energy; the two processes together form an energy cycle.
core.h: Energy transfer: why photosynthesis is endothermic
core.p: A reaction is endothermic if it takes in energy from the surroundings. In photosynthesis the energy is absorbed as **light** and stored as **chemical energy** in the bonds of glucose. This is the reverse of respiration, which releases that energy. Linking this to the energy-change ideas in chemistry shows why the energy stored in food originally came from the Sun.

bullets: Use the **6 : 6 : 1 : 6** mole ratio: 6 molecules of CO₂ give 1 of glucose and 6 of O₂.
**Mass check:** 6CO₂ = 6 × 44 = 264; 6H₂O = 6 × 18 = 108; total 372. Glucose = 180; 6O₂ = 6 × 32 = 192; total 372, so mass is conserved.
Interpret data about **oxygen production** or **CO₂ uptake** as a measure of the rate.
Evaluate experiments: identify variables, suggest improvements, comment on reliability (repeats, mean) and validity.
Explain why the energy in food comes ultimately from the Sun, with correct use of 'transferred'.
Be ready to use data (graphs) from the limiting factors topic that builds on this equation.
core.p: Higher tier questions on photosynthesis often combine the equation with calculations, graphs or data. You may be asked for the amounts of reactants and products, to rearrange or interpret data about rate, or to evaluate a method. Be precise with ratios from the balanced equation and with units.

exam: **1 mark:** recall facts, for example 'carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen' or 'photosynthesis is endothermic'.
**Word/symbol equations (2 marks):** reactants and products correct (1), balanced with numbers and formulas correct (1); write 'light' above the arrow.
**'Describe the starch test' (4 to 5 marks):** boil to kill/soften, ethanol in hot water bath to remove chlorophyll, rinse, add iodine, blue-black = starch; include the safety point.
**'Explain' questions:** link structure to function, for example 'palisade cells have many chloroplasts to absorb more light for photosynthesis'.
**Uses of glucose (3 to 4 marks):** respiration, starch for storage, cellulose for cell walls, fats/oils for storage, amino acids/proteins with nitrate ions.
**Leaf adaptation questions:** name the feature (thin, flat, air spaces, stomata) and the function (short diffusion path, large area for light, gas exchange).
**Command word 'suggest':** use the scenario given, for example a variegated leaf or a plant kept in the dark.
**Evaluate experiments:** mention destarching, controls, one independent variable, repeats and means for reliability.
**Use precise terms:** 'transferred from the environment', 'chloroplasts', 'chlorophyll absorbs light', 'stomata', 'diffusion'.
**Link to other topics:** respiration, food chains and biomass, the carbon cycle, limiting factors; extended answers earn marks for these links.

mistakes.r: Photosynthesis takes IN carbon dioxide and water and gives OUT oxygen (and glucose).
mistakes.w: Plants take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

mistakes.r: It is endothermic: energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.
Plants respire all the time; they photosynthesise only when there is light.
Light energy and chlorophyll are conditions/catalyst-like requirements written on the arrow, not reactants.
mistakes.w: Sunlight or chlorophyll written as a reactant.

mistakes.r: Plants make their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis; the soil provides water and mineral ions.
mistakes.w: Plants get their food from the soil.

mistakes.r: It only happens in cells with chloroplasts; root cells have none.
mistakes.w: Photosynthesis happens in all plant cells.

mistakes.r: Ethanol is flammable: heat it in a hot water bath with the Bunsen burner turned off.
mistakes.w: Using ethanol over a flame in the starch test.

mistakes.r: Iodine tests for starch (blue-black); Benedict’s solution tests for sugars such as glucose.

mistakes.w: Unbalanced equation: CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂.

summary: You must know that **photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction** in which **energy is transferred from the environment (light) to the chloroplasts**, using it to react **carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen**. You need the word and balanced symbol equations, where it happens, and what plants do with the glucose. Photosynthesis is the starting point of nearly all food chains and produces the oxygen in our atmosphere.

terms.d: An endothermic reaction in which energy is transferred from the environment to chloroplasts by light; carbon dioxide and water react to produce glucose and oxygen.
A reaction that transfers energy from the surroundings to the reacting chemicals, so the surroundings get colder.
A sub-cellular structure in plant and algal cells that contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis.
The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
A simple sugar (C₆H₁₂O₆) made in photosynthesis and used in respiration or converted into other substances.
An organism, such as a green plant or alga, that makes its own food by photosynthesis and begins a food chain.
Pores in the epidermis of a leaf, mostly on the underside, through which gases diffuse in and out.
Pairs of cells that surround each stoma and open or close it.
A layer of tightly packed, column-shaped leaf cells containing many chloroplasts where most photosynthesis occurs.
A leaf layer with air spaces that allow gases to diffuse through the leaf.
Plant tissue that transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves.
Plant tissue that transports dissolved sugars (sucrose) around the plant.
An insoluble carbohydrate made from glucose and used by plants as a storage substance; turns iodine blue-black.
A carbohydrate made from glucose that forms plant cell walls.
Mineral ions absorbed from the soil that plants combine with glucose to make amino acids and proteins.
A leaf with green areas containing chlorophyll and white areas without it.

worked.ans: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (light, chlorophyll). It is endothermic because energy is transferred from the environment (light) to the chloroplasts and stored in glucose.
worked.q: Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis and state why it is described as endothermic. (3 marks)
steps: Reactants: carbon dioxide CO₂ and water H₂O. Products: glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ and oxygen O₂.
Balance carbon: 6 CO₂. Balance hydrogen: 6 H₂O gives 12 H. Oxygen: left 12 + 6 = 18; right 6 + 12 = 18 with 6 O₂.
Endothermic means energy taken in from the surroundings.

worked.q: A plant makes 90 g of glucose. Using relative formula masses (CO₂ = 44, O₂ = 32, glucose = 180), calculate the mass of oxygen released. (Higher tier, 3 marks)
steps: 180 g of glucose is produced with 6 × 32 = 192 g of oxygen (from the equation).
90 g is half of 180 g, so the oxygen is half of 192 g.

worked.ans: Only the green areas turn blue-black because they have chlorophyll, so they photosynthesise and store the glucose as starch; the white areas have no chlorophyll, cannot photosynthesise, and stay orange-brown.
worked.q: A variegated leaf (green and white) is destarched, left in light for 6 hours then tested for starch. Describe and explain the expected results. (4 marks)
steps: Describe: the green areas turn blue-black with iodine; the white areas stay orange-brown.
Explain: green areas contain chlorophyll in chloroplasts, which absorbs light for photosynthesis.
Link: glucose made is converted to starch for storage, so starch is found only where photosynthesis occurred.
White areas have no chlorophyll, so no photosynthesis and no starch.
